items.readable_text:
Content:
Given an equation involving complex numbers, we can always equate real and imaginary parts to give two separate equations.

Content:
For example, suppose we're given the equation
[MATH: 2 + 9 \textrm{i} = 2x + 3y \textrm{i}.]

Content:
The real part of [MATH: 2 + 9 \textrm{i}] is [MATH: 2,] and the real part of [MATH: 2x + 3y \textrm{i}] is [MATH: 2x.] Equating the real parts, we get

Content:
[MATH: 2|= 2x; x|= 1.]

Content:
The imaginary part of [MATH: 2 + 9 \textrm{i}] is [MATH: 9,] and the imaginary part of [MATH: 2x + 3y \textrm{i}] is [MATH: 3y.] Equating the imaginary parts, we get

Content:
[MATH: 9|= 3y; y|= 3.]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: x=1] and [MATH: y=3.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we multiply both sides of the equation by [MATH: 1+2\textrm{i}] to get rid of the fraction and isolate the variables:

[MATH: 2 − 3\textrm{i}|= (p − 2q\textrm{i})/(1 + 2\textrm{i}); (2 − 3\textrm{i})(1 + 2\textrm{i})|= p − 2q\textrm{i}; 2 + 4\textrm{i} − 3\textrm{i} − 6\textrm{i}^{2}|= p − 2q\textrm{i}; 2 + \textrm{i} − 6(− 1)|= p − 2q\textrm{i}; 8 + \textrm{i}|= p − 2q\textrm{i}]

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

  • Equating the real parts, we get [MATH: 8 = p.]

  • Equating the imaginary parts, we get [MATH: 1|= − 2q; q|= − (1)/(2).]

Therefore, [MATH: p=8] and [MATH: q = -\dfrac{1}{2}.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we divide both sides of the equation by [MATH: 1+\textrm{i}] to isolate the variables:

[MATH: 3 + 5\textrm{i}|= (p + \textrm{i}q)(1 + \textrm{i}); (3 + 5\textrm{i})/(1 + \textrm{i})|= p + \textrm{i}q]

Now, to simplify the fraction on the left-hand side, we multiply the numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator:

[MATH: ((3 + 5\textrm{i})(1 − \textrm{i}))/((1 + \textrm{i})(1 − \textrm{i}))|= p + \textrm{i}q; (3 − 3\textrm{i} + 5\textrm{i} − 5\textrm{i}^{2})/(1^{2} − \textrm{i}^{2})|= p + \textrm{i}q; (3 + 2\textrm{i} − 5(− 1))/(1 − (− 1))|= p + \textrm{i}q; (8 + 2\textrm{i})/(2)|= p + \textrm{i}q; 4 + \textrm{i}|= p + \textrm{i}q]

Now, we can equate the real parts and the imaginary parts separately.

  • Equating the real parts, we get [MATH: 4=p.]

  • Equating the imaginary parts, we get [MATH: 1=q.]

Therefore, [MATH: p=4] and [MATH: q=1.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Given an equation involving complex numbers, we can always equate real and imaginary parts to give two separate equations.

Content:
For example, suppose we're given the equation
[MATH: 2 + 9 \textrm{i} = 2x + 3y \textrm{i}.]

Content:
The real part of [MATH: 2 + 9 \textrm{i}] is [MATH: 2,] and the real part of [MATH: 2x + 3y \textrm{i}] is [MATH: 2x.] Equating the real parts, we get

Content:
[MATH: 2|= 2x; x|= 1.]

Content:
The imaginary part of [MATH: 2 + 9 \textrm{i}] is [MATH: 9,] and the imaginary part of [MATH: 2x + 3y \textrm{i}] is [MATH: 3y.] Equating the imaginary parts, we get

Content:
[MATH: 9|= 3y; y|= 3.]

Content:
Therefore, [MATH: x=1] and [MATH: y=3.]

---

[MATH: 2 = b]
Therefore, [MATH: a=3] and [MATH: b=2.]
